title: Disseminating China’s vision: A corpus-assisted discourse analysis of “a community with a shared future” in Australian mainstream media
content:
by Yuxin Zhou, Xiaoqian Li

The concept of “a community with a shared future” (CSF) constitutes a cornerstone of China’s contemporary diplomacy. Examining its reception in Australian mainstream media offers critical insights into the global resonance and cross-cultural mediation of Chinese political discourse. Drawing on a specialized corpus of 207 Australian news reports retrieved from the Factiva database (2013–2023), comprising 277,834 tokens, this study employs a corpus-assisted discourse analysis approach to examine the discursive construction of CSF. The analysis investigates the concept across four key dimensions: diachronic frequency, English renderings, thematic focus, and media stance. Findings reveal a fluctuating yet upward trajectory in coverage, significantly punctuated by major geopolitical events. Diachronically, media translations evolved from “common destiny” to “shared future”, broadly aligning with the official English rendering used in Chinese diplomatic discourse. Thematically, LDA topic modeling identified four recurring themes: China’s international influence, domestic politics and leadership, China-Australia relations, and global development and cooperation. Media stance analysis reveals a more differentiated picture than aggregate figures suggest: while the overall corpus shows 67.3% positive, 19.3% neutral, and 13.4% negative segments (n = 254 annotated segments), this distribution is heavily influenced by syndicated content. Among original Australian reporting only (n = 128 segments), the distribution is more balanced: 46.1% positive, 27.3% neutral, and 26.6% negative. In this dataset, all 34 negative segments occur in original rather than syndicated reports, indicating that skepticism framings are concentrated in domestically produced coverage. The study concludes that while Australian media increasingly engages with this diplomatic vision, Australia’s specific geopolitical positioning within the Western alliance system appears to shape the conditions of its reception. The paper discusses implications for understanding how Chinese diplomatic discourse is mediated in liberal democratic contexts, while cautioning against over-generalization beyond the Australian case.
